passages.t: Priests and Levites across the generations
passages.happening:
‘Now these are the priests and Levites who went up with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and with Jeshua’ (verse 1). The chapter names them (verses 1-9). It traces the line of high priests: ‘Jeshua was the father of Joiakim, Joiakim was the father of Eliashib, Eliashib was the father of Joiada’ (verse 10), and Joiada's line runs on to Jonathan and Jaddua (verse 11).

Then come the heads of the priestly families in the days of Joiakim (verses 12-21), a note that the Levites and priests were recorded in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan and Jaddua, ‘during the reign of Darius the Persian’ (verse 22), and the leaders of the Levites, who stood across from one another ‘to give praise and thanksgiving as one section alternated with the other, as prescribed by David the man of God’ (verse 24). They served in the days of Joiakim, and ‘in the days of Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe’ (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The lists connect the present generation to the first returnees under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, nearly a century earlier. The worship now offered stands in a line with the worship restored at the return.

The high priests run from Jeshua, the priest of the first return, through Joiakim, to Eliashib, Nehemiah's contemporary (3:1), and on to Joiada, Jonathan and Jaddua. An Aramaic letter from the Jewish community at Elephantine in Egypt, dated 407 BC, names Johanan as high priest in Jerusalem, which fits the Johanan of verses 22 and 23.

Darius the Persian in verse 22 is identified by many scholars as Darius II, who reigned from about 423 to 404 BC; others suggest Darius III, the last Persian king. Either way, the lists reach beyond Nehemiah's own time.

The singers stood in two sections facing each other, answering one another in praise. The book traces the order of the singers back to David, as Chronicles does.
passages.later: The first return is told in Ezra: ‘accompanied by Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah’ (Ezra 2:2). And Chronicles credits David with setting the singers in their order (1 Chronicles 25:1).
passages.hard:
If the lists run to Jaddua and a later Darius, how can Nehemiah have written them?

Verses 10, 11 and 22 carry the priestly lists past Nehemiah's lifetime, perhaps into the late fifth or even the fourth century BC. Most scholars take this as a sign that Ezra and Nehemiah were put together from several sources, Nehemiah's own memoir, official lists and temple records, by an editor or editors working after Nehemiah's death. That view does not question Nehemiah's first-person account, which is plainly his. It recognizes that the book in its present form was finished later.

Jewish tradition treated Ezra and Nehemiah as one book, and some older interpreters credited Ezra with putting it together, which would limit how late the lists could run. Others, who take the Darius of verse 22 as Darius II, see the lists as updated only a generation after Nehemiah. The Bible does not claim that Nehemiah wrote every line of the book that bears his name, and ancient records were often brought up to date by later scribes.
passages.asks: The lists remember priests and singers across four or five generations. Ask who handed the faith on to the people who handed it on to you. And ask what you are handing on, and to whom.

passages.happening:
‘At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, the Levites were sought out from all their homes and brought to Jerusalem to celebrate the joyous dedication with thanksgiving and singing, accompanied by cymbals, harps, and lyres’ (verse 27). The singers gather from the villages they had built around the city. ‘After the priests and Levites had purified themselves, they purified the people, the gates, and the wall’ (verse 30).

‘Then I brought the leaders of Judah up on the wall, and I appointed two great thanksgiving choirs’ (verse 31). One goes to the right along the top of the wall, toward the Dung Gate, with priests blowing trumpets and Levites playing instruments, and ‘Ezra the scribe led the procession’ (verse 36). The other goes to the left, ‘and I followed it with half the people along the top of the wall’ (verse 38). The two choirs meet and stand in the house of God (verse 40).

‘On that day they offered great sacrifices, rejoicing because God had given them great joy. The women and children also rejoiced, so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard from afar’ (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
This is the high point of the book. The wall finished in chapter 6, the city filled in chapter 11 and the people recommitted to God's law in chapters 8 to 10 all come together in one celebration.

Dedicating a wall was a religious act. It marked the wall as belonging to God. The word is chanukkah, the word used for the dedication of Solomon's temple and of the second temple, and the source of the name Hanukkah. Before the procession, the priests and Levites purify themselves, and then the people, the gates and the wall. Those who lead others in worship are cleansed first.

The procession is carefully described. One choir goes one way with Ezra leading, the other the opposite way with Nehemiah following, and they meet at the temple: a picture of the whole city circled by thanksgiving and brought to the house of God.

The words for joy and rejoicing crowd into verse 43, five times in one verse in Hebrew. And the joy was heard from afar, by the same neighbors who had mocked the builders. Ezra's book had ended its first great scene with a sound heard far off, of joy and weeping mixed together. This sound is joy.
passages.later: A psalm sings of the same city: ‘The LORD builds up Jerusalem; He gathers the exiles of Israel’ (Psalm 147:2). At the first temple's foundation, in Ezra's book, ‘the sound was heard from afar’ (Ezra 3:13), with weeping mixed in.
passages.asks: The whole city walked the wall giving thanks, and the children's joy was heard far off. Ask when you last gave thanks to God together with others, out loud. And ask what joy God has given you that others ought to hear.

passages.happening:
‘And on that same day men were appointed over the rooms that housed the supplies, contributions, firstfruits, and tithes’ (verse 44). The portions the law set aside for the priests and Levites were gathered there from the fields of the villages, ‘because Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who were serving’ (verse 44).

The priests and Levites, singers and gatekeepers do their service as David and Solomon had prescribed (verse 45). ‘So in the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, all Israel contributed the daily portions for the singers and gatekeepers’ (verse 47).
passages.hearers:
The storerooms held the tithes and offerings on which the priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers depended, since they did not farm land of their own. The book sees to the plain work behind the joy: someone has to keep the stores, and everyone has to give.

The section looks back to David and Asaph, who first set singers and songs of thanksgiving in order, and it sets the days of Zerubbabel and of Nehemiah side by side, the first return and the present.

It is a picture of things as they should be. The next chapter shows how quickly it slipped.
passages.later: The law gave the Levites the tithe because they had no land: ‘Behold, I have given to the Levites all the tithes in Israel as an inheritance in return for the work they do’ (Numbers 18:21). Malachi, probably from about the same time, calls the people to ‘Bring the full tithe into the storehouse’ (Malachi 3:10).
passages.asks: The people gave gladly, because they rejoiced over those who served. Ask how you support those who lead the worship and care of your church. And ask whether your giving comes from duty or from joy.
